Cora forgot how to breathe. For six months, the captain had been nothing more than a ghost of light against the horizon, a shared rhythm in the dark. Now, the woman was real, smelling of saltwater, rain, and diesel fuel, her storm-grey eyes locked onto Cora’s with terrifying intensity.

"You're... you're real," Cora managed, her voice trembling above the howl of the wind outside.

"Captain Maeve," the woman said, stepping into the warm glow of the lantern room. Water trickled from the brim of her cap onto the worn hardwood floor. She held out the brass compass, her fingers brushing Cora’s as Cora took it. The metal was cool, but the spot where Maeve’s hand had rested was warm. 

Engraved on the tarnished casing were the exact latitude and longitude of Cora's lantern room—along with three simple dots and three dashes. *Save Our Souls.*

"I bought it in Lisbon three years ago," Maeve said softly, slipping off her dripping coat. Beneath it, her shoulders were broad, her posture tired yet resolute. "I never knew whose coordinates they were until your beam started singing in code. You kept me off the rocks, Cora. In more ways than one."

Cora grabbed a dry wool blanket from her cot and wrapped it around Maeve’s shoulders. As she tucked the edges tight, their faces were inches apart. Maeve reached up, her thumb gently wiping a stray tear from Cora’s cheek. The silence between them wasn't cold like the storm outside; it was heavy with everything they had whispered across miles of empty ocean.

"I thought I was just passing the time," Cora whispered, leaning into Maeve's touch. "I didn't know I was guiding you home."

Maeve offered a soft, crooked smile, pulling Cora closer into the warmth of the blanket. "Home is where the light is."

Outside, the gale battered the glass, but inside, time seemed to stop. Yet, down at the harbor, Maeve’s cargo ship was scheduled to set sail again at dawn.

Come back for the next part tomorrow.
